column1:
User moves to a new desk. Ethernet shows 169.254.x.x, but Wi‑Fi works immediately. What is the MOST likely cause?

A. DHCP server outage
B. Wrong VLAN or port configuration on the wired switch port
C. DNS misconfiguration
D. Faulty NIC
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (Ethernet & Wi‑Fi)
ipconfig /renew (Ethernet)

What it checks:
Whether DHCP works on Wi‑Fi but not on Ethernet and whether the wired adapter can reach DHCP.

Why it works:
If DHCP works on Wi‑Fi, the DHCP server and OS are fine; the wired port/VLAN is suspect.

Success indicates:
Ethernet receives valid IP after port/VLAN fix.

Failure indicates:
Ethernet remains APIPA; DHCP unreachable from that port/VLAN.

Common pitfall:
Assuming DHCP is down because one adapter fails.

column1:
User plugs into a conference room jack and receives 169.254.x.x. Back at their desk, Ethernet works normally. What does this MOST strongly indicate?

A. Intermittent DHCP server failure
B. Conference room port mapped to a VLAN without DHCP access
C. Corrupt network driver
D. DNS issue
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (conference room)
ipconfig /all (desk)

What it checks:
IP range and DHCP behavior by physical location.

Why it works:
Location‑specific APIPA points to port/VLAN configuration, not endpoint failure.

Success indicates:
Valid IP obtained after port/VLAN correction.

Failure indicates:
APIPA persists only on conference room ports.

Common pitfall:
Reinstalling drivers instead of correlating to location.

column1:
User docks their laptop and immediately receives 169.254.x.x on Ethernet. Undocked Wi‑Fi works. What is the BEST next conclusion?

A. Laptop hardware failure
B. Dock Ethernet path is mapped to wrong VLAN or disabled port
C. DNS cache corruption
D. DHCP scope exhaustion
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (docked)
ipconfig /all (Wi‑Fi)

What it checks:
Whether DHCP works via Wi‑Fi but not via dock Ethernet.

Why it works:
Different physical paths map to different switch ports/VLANs.

Success indicates:
Valid IP after correcting dock port/VLAN.

Failure indicates:
APIPA only when docked.

Common pitfall:
Replacing the laptop when the issue is the dock/port.

column1:
User plugs PC into phone passthrough port and gets 169.254.x.x. Phone itself works. What is MOST likely?

A. DHCP server is down
B. Voice VLAN configured, data VLAN missing or misconfigured
C. DNS server issue
D. User error
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
Check adapter DHCP enabled

What it checks:
Whether the data VLAN is properly tagged/passed through the phone.

Why it works:
Phones often tag voice VLANs; PC relies on correct data VLAN passthrough.

Success indicates:
PC receives valid IP after phone or port configuration fix.

Failure indicates:
PC remains APIPA while phone works.

Common pitfall:
Assuming phone connectivity guarantees PC connectivity.

column1:
Multiple users on one floor receive 169.254.x.x, while other floors work normally. What does this suggest FIRST?

A. Global DHCP outage
B. Missing DHCP relay or VLAN misconfiguration on that floor
C. DNS failure
D. Malware spread
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (affected floor)
ipconfig /all (working floor)

What it checks:
DHCP reachability by VLAN or floor.

Why it works:
Floor‑specific failures indicate VLAN/relay configuration issues.

Success indicates:
Valid IPs after relay/VLAN fix.

Failure indicates:
APIPA persists only on affected floor.

Common pitfall:
Escalating to DHCP server team without checking VLANs.

column1:
User reports APIPA appears only after reboot, but not after sleep. What is a plausible infrastructure explanation?

A. Random Windows bug
B. Port security or switch timing issue during boot
C. DNS misconfiguration
D. Expired certificate
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all after reboot
ipconfig /renew

What it checks:
DHCP behavior during full link renegotiation.

Why it works:
Switch port policies can block DHCP briefly during boot.

Success indicates:
Valid IP obtained after port config or delay adjustment.

Failure indicates:
APIPA appears consistently on reboot.

Common pitfall:
Assuming OS corruption.

column1:
User gets APIPA on wired, but receives a valid IP on guest Wi‑Fi. What is the BEST interpretation?

A. DHCP server partially down
B. Wired VLAN lacks DHCP access; guest Wi‑Fi has separate DHCP
C. DNS issue
D. Wrong password
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (wired)
ipconfig /all (Wi‑Fi)

What it checks:
DHCP behavior across network segments.

Why it works:
Different segments have different DHCP paths.

Success indicates:
Wired works after VLAN/relay fix.

Failure indicates:
Wired remains APIPA; Wi‑Fi unaffected.

Common pitfall:
Assuming DHCP is global.

column1:
User shows 169.254.x.x with DHCP Enabled = Yes. Other users are online. What should you suspect FIRST?

A. DHCP server outage
B. Client VLAN/port cannot reach DHCP
C. DNS cache issue
D. Subnet mask problem
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
ipconfig /renew

What it checks:
Whether DHCP is enabled but unreachable from the client.

Why it works:
APIPA with DHCP enabled indicates reachability issue, not disabled DHCP.

Success indicates:
Valid IP after port/VLAN correction.

Failure indicates:
Renew continues to fail.

Common pitfall:
Restarting DHCP service unnecessarily.

column1:
APIPA appears immediately after a network maintenance window. What is a likely cause?

A. User error
B. Switch/VLAN changes removed DHCP relay or access
C. DNS outage
D. Browser issue
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
Compare with known‑good VLAN

What it checks:
DHCP reachability after infrastructure changes.

Why it works:
Maintenance often affects VLAN or relay configs.

Success indicates:
Valid IP restored after rollback/fix.

Failure indicates:
APIPA persists post‑maintenance.

Common pitfall:
Assuming coincidence.

column1:
APIPA affects only one VLAN; others receive valid IPs. What does this MOST strongly indicate?

A. DHCP scope exhaustion
B. Missing or misconfigured DHCP relay on that VLAN
C. DNS failure
D. NIC driver issue
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (affected VLAN)
ipconfig /all (working VLAN)

What it checks:
DHCP reachability by VLAN.

Why it works:
Relays forward DHCP across VLANs; missing relay breaks DHCP for that segment.

Success indicates:
Valid IP after relay configuration.

Failure indicates:
APIPA continues on that VLAN.

Common pitfall:
Blaming DHCP server instead of relay.

column1:
User has a valid IP address but the Default Gateway field is blank. What is the MOST likely cause?

A. DNS server outage
B. DHCP scope missing gateway option
C. Corrupt NIC driver
D. Firewall blocking traffic
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
Whether a default gateway was provided by DHCP.

Why it works:
DHCP option 003 provides the gateway; if missing, routing fails.

Success indicates:
Gateway appears after DHCP scope correction.

Failure indicates:
Clients cannot route off subnet.

Common pitfall:
Chasing DNS before verifying gateway.

column1:
User has a valid IP and gateway configured, but cannot reach any external networks. What is the FIRST test?

A. nslookup google.com
B. ping default gateway
C. flush DNS
D. reboot
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ping <default-gateway>

What it checks:
Whether the client can reach its first routing hop.

Why it works:
Gateway reachability validates VLAN placement and L2 connectivity.

Success indicates:
Gateway replies consistently.

Failure indicates:
Gateway unreachable due to wrong VLAN or port.

Common pitfall:
Testing DNS before routing.

column1:
User’s gateway pings successfully, but internet access fails. What does this MOST likely indicate?

A. DNS failure
B. Upstream routing or firewall issue beyond the gateway
C. DHCP server outage
D. NIC failure
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ping 8.8.8.8

What it checks:
Whether traffic routes beyond the local gateway.

Why it works:
Confirms whether the issue is upstream of the gateway.

Success indicates:
8.8.8.8 replies after routing fix.

Failure indicates:
Upstream routing blocked.

Common pitfall:
Assuming gateway reachability equals full connectivity.

column1:
User receives a valid IP but the gateway IP does not match the site standard. What should you suspect FIRST?

A. DNS misconfiguration
B. Wrong DHCP scope or VLAN
C. Malware infection
D. OS corruption
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
Compare with known-good

What it checks:
Whether the gateway matches expected network design.

Why it works:
Incorrect scope or VLAN hands out wrong gateway.

Success indicates:
Correct gateway after scope/VLAN fix.

Failure indicates:
Gateway mismatch persists.

Common pitfall:
Trusting any gateway value without validation.

column1:
User can ping the gateway but cannot reach internal servers. Internet access also fails. What is MOST likely?

A. DNS issue
B. Routing table or ACL issue at the gateway
C. DHCP outage
D. Expired user credentials
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ping <gateway>
tracert <internal-ip>

What it checks:
Whether traffic is routed or blocked beyond the gateway.

Why it works:
Gateway may respond but block or misroute traffic.

Success indicates:
Traffic routes correctly after fix.

Failure indicates:
Traffic stops at gateway.

Common pitfall:
Stopping troubleshooting at a successful gateway ping.

column1:
Gateway responds intermittently depending on desk location. What does this suggest?

A. Random OS bug
B. Inconsistent VLAN or switch port configuration
C. DNS instability
D. Browser issue
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ping <gateway>
ipconfig /all (multiple locations)

What it checks:
Gateway reachability tied to physical port.

Why it works:
Different ports may map to different VLANs.

Success indicates:
Stable connectivity after port normalization.

Failure indicates:
Gateway unreachable on some ports.

Common pitfall:
Assuming user device inconsistency.

column1:
User reports that only local subnet resources are reachable. Gateway is configured. What is MOST likely wrong?

A. DNS resolution
B. Gateway routing misconfiguration
C. DHCP lease expired
D. NIC duplex mismatch
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ping <gateway>
tracert <external-ip>

What it checks:
Whether routing beyond subnet is functioning.

Why it works:
Misconfigured gateway cannot route external traffic.

Success indicates:
External routing restored after fix.

Failure indicates:
Traffic stops at gateway.

Common pitfall:
Assuming subnet reachability equals routing.

column1:
Gateway is reachable on Wi-Fi but not on Ethernet. What is the BEST conclusion?

A. Laptop hardware issue
B. Wired VLAN or switch port issue
C. DNS cache corruption
D. DHCP server down
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (Wi-Fi)
ipconfig /all (Ethernet)
ping <gateway>

What it checks:
Gateway reachability across adapters.

Why it works:
Different adapters map to different VLANs.

Success indicates:
Ethernet gateway reachable after port fix.

Failure indicates:
Ethernet gateway unreachable.

Common pitfall:
Reinstalling OS instead of checking port.

column1:
User’s gateway changes after a DHCP renew. What does this MOST likely indicate?

A. Normal behavior
B. Multiple DHCP servers or overlapping scopes
C. DNS issue
D. Windows bug
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /release
ipconfig /renew

What it checks:
Whether multiple gateways are handed out.

Why it works:
Multiple DHCP sources cause inconsistent configs.

Success indicates:
Single consistent gateway after cleanup.

Failure indicates:
Gateway alternates between renewals.

Common pitfall:
Ignoring DHCP conflicts.

column1:
Gateway responds, DNS resolves, but applications still fail intermittently. What should you suspect?

A. DNS outage
B. Gateway ACL or firewall rules
C. DHCP exhaustion
D. Browser cache
column2:
Correct Answer: B

Command(s) to run:
ping <gateway>
tracert <app-server>

What it checks:
Whether traffic is selectively blocked.

Why it works:
ACLs can allow ICMP but block application traffic.

Success indicates:
Applications work after ACL update.

Failure indicates:
App traffic blocked while pings succeed.

Common pitfall:
Assuming ICMP success equals app success.

column1:
User has a valid IP address, but the IP range does not match the site standard. Internet works, internal apps fail. What is MOST likely?

A. Expired DHCP lease
B. DNS server outage
C. Client is on the wrong VLAN
D. Laptop hardware failure
column2:
Correct Answer: C. Client is on the wrong VLAN

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
ping <internal-ip>

What it checks:
IP range, gateway, and internal reachability

Why it works:
Wrong VLANs can allow limited access while blocking internal routes

Success indicates:
IP range corrected after VLAN change

Failure indicates:
Internal access remains blocked

Common pitfall:
Assuming internet access means correct VLAN

column1:
User receives a valid IP from a guest network while plugged into a corporate jack. What does this indicate?

A. Guest VLAN mapped to the port
B. Correct VLAN assignment
C. DNS misconfiguration
D. Corrupt NIC driver
column2:
Correct Answer: A. Guest VLAN mapped to the port

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
Compare with known-good

What it checks:
DHCP server and IP range source

Why it works:
Guest VLANs hand out different IP ranges

Success indicates:
Correct corporate IP after port fix

Failure indicates:
Client remains on guest range

Common pitfall:
Trusting physical jack labels

column1:
User has a valid IP. DHCP Server listed is a firewall instead of the normal Windows server. What should you suspect?

A. Wrong VLAN or scope
B. Malware
C. Normal configuration
D. DNS failure
column2:
Correct Answer: A. Wrong VLAN or scope

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
DHCP server identity

Why it works:
Different VLANs may use different DHCP sources

Success indicates:
Correct DHCP server after VLAN fix

Failure indicates:
Unexpected DHCP server persists

Common pitfall:
Ignoring DHCP server field

column1:
User has valid IP and DNS servers, but cannot access internal resources. Internet works. What is MOST likely?

A. DNS cache issue
B. Expired credentials
C. Isolated or restricted VLAN
D. Broken NIC
column2:
Correct Answer: C. Isolated or restricted VLAN

Command(s) to run:
ping 8.8.8.8
ping <internal-ip>

What it checks:
External vs internal routing

Why it works:
Isolated VLANs allow internet only

Success indicates:
Internal access restored after VLAN change

Failure indicates:
Internal blocked while internet works

Common pitfall:
Assuming DNS is at fault

column1:
Two users sit next to each other. One works, one does not. Both have valid IPs. What should you check FIRST?

A. Browser cache
B. Reimage the failing PC
C. Compare IP ranges and gateways
D. Reset passwords
column2:
Correct Answer: C. Compare IP ranges and gateways

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (both systems)

What it checks:
VLAN placement differences

Why it works:
Different VLANs can exist on adjacent ports

Success indicates:
Configs align after port fix

Failure indicates:
Mismatch persists

Common pitfall:
Assuming proximity means same VLAN

column1:
User receives a valid IP, but subnet mask does not match site standard. What does this usually indicate?

A. DNS failure
B. Bad NIC
C. Wrong DHCP scope
D. Expired lease
column2:
Correct Answer: C. Wrong DHCP scope

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
Subnet mask handed out by DHCP

Why it works:
Incorrect scope options cause routing issues

Success indicates:
Correct mask after scope fix

Failure indicates:
Mask remains incorrect

Common pitfall:
Ignoring subnet mask

column1:
User has valid IP, correct gateway, but DNS suffix is unexpected. Internal name resolution fails. Why?

A. Browser issue
B. Hardware failure
C. Expired DHCP lease
D. Wrong VLAN policy
column2:
Correct Answer: D. Wrong VLAN policy

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
nslookup internal-name

What it checks:
DNS suffix and resolution behavior

Why it works:
Different VLANs apply different DNS policies

Success indicates:
Correct suffix restores resolution

Failure indicates:
Resolution continues to fail

Common pitfall:
Assuming DNS servers alone are sufficient

column1:
After a desk move, user has valid IP but is placed on the voice VLAN. What symptom is MOST likely?

A. APIPA address
B. Limited or no data access
C. Full network access
D. Improved performance
column2:
Correct Answer: B. Limited or no data access

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
IP range and VLAN behavior

Why it works:
Voice VLANs restrict data traffic

Success indicates:
Access restored after correct VLAN assignment

Failure indicates:
Data access remains limited

Common pitfall:
Assuming valid IP means correct VLAN

column1:
User has valid IP, correct DNS servers, but cannot reach internal apps. Gateway is reachable. What is MOST likely?

A. Expired credentials
B. ACL-restricted VLAN
C. DNS outage
D. NIC failure
column2:
Correct Answer: B. ACL-restricted VLAN

Command(s) to run:
ping <gateway>
tracert <internal-ip>

What it checks:
Routing vs ACL behavior

Why it works:
ACLs may allow ICMP but block apps

Success indicates:
Apps work after ACL fix

Failure indicates:
Apps remain blocked

Common pitfall:
Stopping after successful ping

column1:
User has valid IP but cannot access resources expected for their department. Others can. What should you suspect?

A. Wrong VLAN assignment
B. DHCP outage
C. DNS cache corruption
D. User error
column2:
Correct Answer: A. Wrong VLAN assignment

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
Compare with department peer

What it checks:
VLAN assignment by role/location

Why it works:
Different VLANs grant different access scopes

Success indicates:
Correct VLAN restores access

Failure indicates:
Access remains incorrect

Common pitfall:
Assuming all valid IPs are equal

column1:
User moved to a temporary desk. Network worked at old desk, now they get the wrong IP range. What is MOST likely?

A. Wrong switch port/VLAN assignment at the new desk
B. Browser problem
C. Expired credentials
D. DNS cache issue
column2:
Correct Answer: A. Wrong switch port/VLAN assignment at the new desk

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
Compare with known-good at that desk area

What it checks:
IP range/DHCP server differences by location

Why it works:
Hot desks/temporary desks often map to different VLANs

Success indicates:
Correct IP after port/VLAN fix

Failure indicates:
Wrong range persists at that desk

Common pitfall:
Reimaging before validating port/VLAN

column1:
Conference room jack gives valid IP but only internet works; internal resources fail. What does this MOST likely indicate?

A. DHCP server outage
B. DNS is down
C. Corrupt NIC driver
D. Isolated guest VLAN in conference rooms
column2:
Correct Answer: D. Isolated guest VLAN in conference rooms

Command(s) to run:
ping 8.8.8.8
ping <internal-ip>
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
External vs internal routing from that port

Why it works:
Conference rooms may be intentionally segmented

Success indicates:
Internal works after VLAN change

Failure indicates:
Internal blocked while internet works

Common pitfall:
Assuming internal apps are down globally

column1:
User plugs into IP phone passthrough. Phone works, PC gets wrong IP range. What is MOST likely?

A. Phone port tagged for voice VLAN and PC placed incorrectly
B. DNS suffix issue only
C. Windows update pending
D. Normal behavior
column2:
Correct Answer: A. Phone port tagged for voice VLAN and PC placed incorrectly

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all

What it checks:
IP range/DHCP server identity when using phone passthrough

Why it works:
Voice VLAN configurations can misplace the PC into the wrong segment

Success indicates:
Correct IP after phone/port configuration fix

Failure indicates:
Wrong range persists on phone passthrough

Common pitfall:
Assuming phone success means PC is on correct VLAN

column1:
User docks laptop; Ethernet fails, Wi-Fi works. They swap docks and it works. What is MOST likely?

A. DNS misconfiguration
B. Laptop OS corruption
C. DHCP exhaustion
D. Bad dock or dock port patched to wrong VLAN
column2:
Correct Answer: D. Bad dock or dock port patched to wrong VLAN

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (Ethernet)
Compare with working dock

What it checks:
Whether DHCP/VLAN differs between docks

Why it works:
Different docks may be patched to different ports/VLANs or be faulty

Success indicates:
Ethernet works at corrected dock/port

Failure indicates:
Ethernet fails only on one dock

Common pitfall:
Replacing the laptop instead of the dock/port

column1:
Hot-desk environment: user works at desk A but not desk B. Both desks show link lights. What should you do FIRST?

A. Reset the user password
B. Flush DNS cache
C. Reinstall Wi-Fi drivers
D. Compare ipconfig /all between desks
column2:
Correct Answer: D. Compare ipconfig /all between desks

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (desk A)
ipconfig /all (desk B)

What it checks:
VLAN/IP/gateway differences tied to physical ports

Why it works:
Link lights only prove physical connectivity, not VLAN correctness

Success indicates:
Desk B matches Desk A after port fix

Failure indicates:
Desk B shows wrong range/gateway

Common pitfall:
Treating link lights as proof the network is 'fine'

column1:
User says wall port label 'DATA' but they get a voice VLAN IP range. What is MOST likely?

A. DHCP server down
B. Browser cache
C. DNS outage
D. Labeling/patching mismatch
column2:
Correct Answer: D. Labeling/patching mismatch

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
Test alternate wall port if available

What it checks:
Whether the port maps to voice VLAN despite labeling

Why it works:
Physical labels can be wrong; patch panel mapping may be incorrect

Success indicates:
Correct VLAN after using correct port or repatch

Failure indicates:
Voice VLAN persists on that jack

Common pitfall:
Assuming physical labels are always accurate

column1:
Patch panel issue suspected: user’s port works, but neighbor’s identical port fails with APIPA. What is BEST next step?

A. Disable firewall
B. Escalate to networking with evidence (ipconfig /all + location)
C. Flush DNS
D. Reinstall OS
column2:
Correct Answer: B. Escalate to networking with evidence (ipconfig /all + location)

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (affected)
ipconfig /all (working)
Document jack/desk ID

What it checks:
Location-specific DHCP/VLAN behavior

Why it works:
Network team needs exact port/jack details to trace patching

Success indicates:
Network team can confirm and correct mapping

Failure indicates:
Issue persists tied to a specific jack/port

Common pitfall:
Escalating without port/jack evidence

column1:
User plugs into an untrusted wall port and gets APIPA. Another nearby port works. What does this MOST likely indicate?

A. DNS server outage
B. That wall port is not patched or is on a VLAN without DHCP
C. Expired lease
D. Bad NIC
column2:
Correct Answer: B. That wall port is not patched or is on a VLAN without DHCP

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
Try alternate port
ipconfig /renew

What it checks:
Whether DHCP works on alternative port and whether APIPA is location-specific

Why it works:
Unpatched/misconfigured ports won’t provide DHCP access

Success indicates:
Valid IP on the working port

Failure indicates:
APIPA persists only on the bad port

Common pitfall:
Assuming it’s a device issue without testing another jack

column1:
Interviewer says: 'The user has an IP address, so DHCP is working.' What is the BEST response?

A. Agree if the gateway responds
B. Change topic to DNS
C. Agree, DHCP is fully working
D. Disagree — DHCP issued an IP but VLAN or routing may still be wrong
column2:
Correct Answer: D. Disagree — DHCP issued an IP but VLAN or routing may still be wrong

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
ping <gateway>

What it checks:
Whether DHCP success implies correct network placement

Why it works:
DHCP lease does not guarantee correct VLAN or routing

Success indicates:
Correct VLAN/gateway verified

Failure indicates:
Client isolated despite valid IP

Common pitfall:
Treating DHCP success as end of troubleshooting

column1:
Interviewer says: 'DNS resolves, so the network is fine.' What is the CORRECT rebuttal?

A. DNS and routing are the same
B. Only applies on Wi-Fi
C. DNS resolution does not guarantee routing or access
D. Agree, name resolution proves connectivity
column2:
Correct Answer: C. DNS resolution does not guarantee routing or access

Command(s) to run:
ping <gateway>
ping <destination-ip>

What it checks:
Routing vs name resolution

Why it works:
DNS can succeed even when routing is broken

Success indicates:
Traffic reaches destination IP

Failure indicates:
Traffic blocked despite name resolution

Common pitfall:
Stopping troubleshooting after nslookup

column1:
Interviewer claims: 'APIPA always means the DHCP server is down.' What should you say?

A. Only true on wired connections
B. APIPA means the client cannot reach DHCP from its network segment
C. Agree
D. Only true on Wi-Fi
column2:
Correct Answer: B. APIPA means the client cannot reach DHCP from its network segment

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
ipconfig /renew

What it checks:
DHCP reachability vs DHCP availability

Why it works:
APIPA reflects reachability, not server status

Success indicates:
Valid IP after VLAN/relay fix

Failure indicates:
APIPA persists on that segment

Common pitfall:
Restarting DHCP without checking VLANs

column1:
Interviewer says: 'If the gateway pings, routing is fine.' What is the BEST correction?

A. Only applies to Wi-Fi
B. Routing issues only affect DNS
C. Agree
D. Gateway ping only proves first hop; ACLs or routing rules may still block traffic
column2:
Correct Answer: D. Gateway ping only proves first hop; ACLs or routing rules may still block traffic

Command(s) to run:
ping <gateway>
tracert <destination>

What it checks:
First-hop vs end-to-end routing

Why it works:
Gateways may respond to ICMP but block other traffic

Success indicates:
Traffic routes correctly end-to-end

Failure indicates:
Traffic stops beyond gateway

Common pitfall:
Stopping after a successful gateway ping

column1:
Interviewer says: 'Works on Wi-Fi, so the laptop is fine.' What is the BEST expanded answer?

A. Disagree, Wi-Fi is unreliable
B. Agree and stop troubleshooting
C. Agree, and focus on the wired port or VLAN
D. Reimage the laptop
column2:
Correct Answer: C. Agree, and focus on the wired port or VLAN

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (Wi-Fi)
ipconfig /all (Ethernet)

What it checks:
Adapter-specific VLAN placement

Why it works:
Different adapters map to different VLANs

Success indicates:
Ethernet works after port fix

Failure indicates:
Ethernet remains broken

Common pitfall:
Ignoring adapter differences

column1:
Interviewer claims: 'If two users are in the same subnet, they must be on the same VLAN.' What is the correct response?

A. Depends on DNS
B. Agree
C. Only true in small networks
D. Disagree — subnets can span multiple VLANs or be misassigned
column2:
Correct Answer: D. Disagree — subnets can span multiple VLANs or be misassigned

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
Compare DHCP server and gateway

What it checks:
Subnet vs VLAN separation

Why it works:
Same subnet does not guarantee same VLAN

Success indicates:
Correct VLAN verified

Failure indicates:
Users isolated despite same subnet

Common pitfall:
Equating IP math with network design

column1:
Interviewer says: 'If internet works, VLAN must be correct.' What is the BEST rebuttal?

A. Agree
B. Only applies on Wi-Fi
C. Disagree — guest or isolated VLANs often allow internet only
D. Only applies on wired
column2:
Correct Answer: C. Disagree — guest or isolated VLANs often allow internet only

Command(s) to run:
ping 8.8.8.8
ping <internal-ip>

What it checks:
External vs internal access

Why it works:
Isolated VLANs commonly allow internet but block internal traffic

Success indicates:
Internal access restored after VLAN change

Failure indicates:
Internal remains blocked

Common pitfall:
Assuming internet access equals full access

column1:
After a desk move, a user gets APIPA on Ethernet, gateway unreachable, but Wi-Fi works. What is the MOST likely root cause?

A. Wired switch port on wrong VLAN or no DHCP access
B. DHCP server outage
C. Laptop NIC failure
D. DNS outage
column2:
Correct Answer: A. Wired switch port on wrong VLAN or no DHCP access

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
ping <gateway>
ipconfig /renew

What it checks:
DHCP reachability and gateway presence on wired vs Wi-Fi

Why it works:
Wi-Fi success proves DHCP and OS are fine; wired port is misconfigured

Success indicates:
Ethernet works after port/VLAN correction

Failure indicates:
APIPA persists only on wired

Common pitfall:
Blaming DHCP server globally

column1:
User has valid IP, wrong gateway, internal access fails, internet intermittently works. What should you suspect FIRST?

A. DNS instability
B. Multiple DHCP servers or overlapping scopes
C. Malware infection
D. NIC power saving
column2:
Correct Answer: B. Multiple DHCP servers or overlapping scopes

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all
ipconfig /release
ipconfig /renew

What it checks:
Gateway consistency across renewals

Why it works:
Multiple DHCP sources can hand out inconsistent gateways

Success indicates:
Single correct gateway after cleanup

Failure indicates:
Gateway changes between renewals

Common pitfall:
Ignoring DHCP conflicts

column1:
Some users on a floor get APIPA, others get valid IPs but wrong access. What is the MOST likely explanation?

A. Random Windows issues
B. Expired credentials
C. VLAN segmentation differences by switch or port group
D. DNS cache corruption
column2:
Correct Answer: C. VLAN segmentation differences by switch or port group

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (multiple users)
Compare by location

What it checks:
DHCP/VLAN behavior across ports

Why it works:
Different VLANs or relays may serve different port groups

Success indicates:
All users receive correct access after normalization

Failure indicates:
Mixed behavior persists

Common pitfall:
Assuming a single cause fits all users

column1:
User works on VPN but not on-site wired network. What does this MOST strongly suggest?

A. VPN client misconfiguration
B. On-site VLAN or routing issue
C. User account restriction
D. DNS failure
column2:
Correct Answer: B. On-site VLAN or routing issue

Command(s) to run:
ipconfig /all (on-site)
ipconfig /all (VPN)

What it checks:
Access differences between network contexts

Why it works:
VPN bypasses local VLAN issues

Success indicates:
On-site access restored after VLAN fix

Failure indicates:
On-site remains broken

Common pitfall:
Troubleshooting VPN when it works

column1:
Multiple symptoms: valid IP, gateway reachable, DNS resolves, but only some internal apps work. What is the BEST next escalation step?

A. Reimage the workstation
B. Restart DHCP service
C. Escalate to network team with tracert and port details
D. Flush DNS cache
column2:
Correct Answer: C. Escalate to network team with tracert and port details

Command(s) to run:
tracert <app-server>
ipconfig /all
Document port/jack

What it checks:
Path and policy enforcement beyond first hop

Why it works:
Network team can trace ACL/routing with evidence

Success indicates:
Apps restored after policy fix

Failure indicates:
Apps remain blocked until escalation

Common pitfall:
Escalating without evidence
